title: Course Project and Teacher's Choice: Latin Poetry

guide.summary: Unit 6 develops the tools for reading Latin poetry closely, scansion of dactylic hexameter and figures of speech, and applies them in the course project, where students interpret project passages and support claims with textual evidence.

sections.heading: Dactylic hexameter
sections.body: Each line has six feet; feet 1–4 may be dactyls (long–short–short) or spondees (long–long), the fifth is usually a dactyl, and the sixth has two syllables (long plus long or short). A syllable is long by nature (long vowel or diphthong) or by position (a short vowel followed by two consonants, which may be in the next word; x and z count as double). Elision drops a final vowel, or vowel + m, before a word starting with a vowel or h (atqu(e) altae). A main pause (caesura) usually falls in the third foot. Spondaic lines feel slow and heavy; dactylic lines feel quick.

sections.heading: Figures of speech
sections.body: Common figures: alliteration (magno misceri murmure, imitating the roar of the sea), assonance, anaphora (repetition at the start of clauses), apostrophe (addressing someone absent: o patria), asyndeton (no conjunctions), polysyndeton (many conjunctions), chiasmus (ABBA arrangement), hyperbaton (separation of words that belong together), synchysis or interlocked word order, the golden line (two adjectives, verb, two nouns: aurea purpuream subnectit fibula vestem), hendiadys (one idea through two nouns), litotes (understatement by double negative), metonymy, synecdoche, personification, simile, tricolon (three-part structure), and enjambment. Always explain the effect: how the device reinforces meaning, emotion, or emphasis.

sections.heading: Course project
sections.body: The course project includes in-class checkpoints: a written draft summary and an interpretive product supported by textual evidence, based on project passages chosen by the teacher. On the exam, Questions 4 and 5 ask short essay questions on a prose passage and a poetry passage connected to the project. Success depends on the same skills as the rest of the course: accurate reading, a clear claim, and specific Latin evidence that is cited, translated or paraphrased, and explained.

sections.heading: Worked example: scanning a line
sections.body: To scan Albanique patres, atque altae moenia Romae, first mark elision: atque before altae loses its final e. Next mark syllables long by nature (Albānī, Rōmae) or by position (Al-, -bā-, the at- of atque). Then fill in the six feet from the end, since the fifth foot is usually a dactyl and the sixth has two syllables: moenĭă Rōmae gives a dactyl and a final spondee. Working backward, you get spondee, dactyl, spondee, spondee, dactyl, spondee. Practice by scanning the first seven lines of the Aeneid and checking with a teacher or a reliable scansion.

sections.heading: Figures of speech with effects
sections.body: Naming a figure earns little credit unless you explain its effect. Chiasmus can emphasize contrast or balance; anaphora creates urgency or emphasis through repetition; apostrophe heightens emotion by addressing someone absent; asyndeton speeds the pace; polysyndeton slows it and suggests accumulation; hyperbaton can create suspense or mirror meaning, as when words for 'surrounding' surround the noun. A golden line, with interlocked adjectives and nouns around a verb, can mirror an image of weaving or fastening. Onomatopoeia and alliteration imitate sounds such as the roar of the sea or galloping horses.

sections.heading: Course project skills
sections.body: The course project asks you to develop an interpretation of passages and support it with textual evidence. Start with a clear claim about meaning or theme, gather specific Latin words and phrases that support it, and explain how each piece of evidence connects to your claim. Draft a summary, revise based on feedback, and present your interpretation in a polished product. These are the same skills tested in the exam's project passage short essays.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: When writing about poetry, combine meter, sound, and imagery. For example, a line with many spondees and long vowels may slow the pace during a moment of grief, while a quick dactylic line may mirror rapid motion. Explain how form reinforces meaning, quote the exact Latin, and translate or paraphrase it. This approach serves both the course project and the exam's poetry project passage essay.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know dactyl, spondee, elision, caesura, enjambment, chiasmus, anaphora, apostrophe, golden line, and hendiadys.

practice.prompt:
Read Aeneid 6.851–853 (Unit 5) and answer both parts, supporting your claims with Latin from the lines.

tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento
(hae tibi erunt artes), pacique imponere morem,

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: How do the grammar and form of the passage reinforce Anchises' message?

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Identify a figure of speech in line 853 and explain its effect.

rubric.description: Identifies how the passage's form (imperative, apostrophe, parallel infinitives) shapes its message.
Cites and explains specific Latin (Romane, memento, the infinitives).
Explains a figure in line 853 and its effect.
Cites parcere subiectis et debellare superbos and explains the antithesis/parallelism.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Anchises addresses the future Roman directly with the vocative Romane and the imperative memento, 'remember', turning prophecy into a command. The infinitives regere, imponere, parcere, and debellare all depend on memento, creating a list of duties that defines the Roman character as one of rule and order. The parenthesis hae tibi erunt artes, 'these will be your arts', contrasts Rome's 'arts' of government with the arts of other peoples.

B. Line 853, parcere subiectis et debellare superbos, uses parallel structure and antithesis: two infinitives each with a dative or accusative object, balancing mercy toward the conquered (subiectis) with force against the proud (superbos). The balance mirrors the ideal of measured power, which is why readers measure Aeneas' final killing of Turnus against it.
